content.content:
**Proposition 40** is a California measure on the November 3, 2026 General Election ballot. It was placed there through petition signatures and would levy a one-time tax on billionaires, with most of the revenue directed to health care.

- **Official title:** "IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE."
- **Official summary:** "Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion." The revenue would be shielded from constitutional rules on school funding and from the spending limit.
- **Yes vote:** "The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth."
- **No vote:** "The state would *not* collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth."
- **Fiscal impact:** Revenue would temporarily rise by tens of billions of dollars, collected across several years from the billionaire wealth tax. It could also reduce annual income tax collections from billionaires by less than $1 billion on an ongoing basis.
- **Election date:** November 3, 2026 (Election Day). Polls run 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Counties start mailing ballots by October 5, 2026, and the voter registration deadline is October 19, 2026.
- **Supporters:** US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
- **Opponents:** California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association

**Arguments**
- **Pro (Yes):** Supporters say Trump cut health care funding to pay for tax breaks for billionaires. They say this cost more than a million Californians their coverage and doubled premiums for millions of others. They argue billionaires should contribute their share instead of leaving the middle class to cover the costs.
- **Con (No):** Opponents call it a flawed plan built around a one-time levy that would hurt the economy and damage the state budget. They point to a loophole that would leave Californians facing taxes they cannot afford, and say the measure "does nothing to lower healthcare costs." They also say it lacks safeguards and accountability.
- The No argument names groups it asks voters to join: California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children's Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, and "Democrats and Republicans."

**Campaign contacts**
- **For:** SEIU-UHW (Suzanne Jimenez), (855) 507-7562, https://yeson40.com/
- **Against:** Californians to Protect Funding for Schools, Healthcare and Public Safety, https://votenoon40.org/

content.content:
**Article date:** October 16, 2019 (updated March 3, 2020). CalMatters fact check by Ben Christopher.

**Bottom line:** The common belief that support fades as the vote nears largely holds up.

- **Dataset:** Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) surveys of "likely voters" covering about 80 initiatives since 1998, tracked from roughly a year before the vote through official results.
- **Average decline:** The yes-minus-no margin fell about 6.6 points per month on average. The article's summary rounds this to about 7. Roughly 71% of measures lost ground, and the rest gained.
- **Election type:** The sharpest falloffs came in low-turnout years without a presidential race. Off-year contests, such as midterm primaries, usually saw drops of more than 10 points. Declines were far milder before general elections, especially presidential ones. Polls also overstated support most in off-year races compared with final results.
- **Spending imbalance:** A separate study of 1976–2004 California ballot campaigns found that those where opponents outspent supporters by more than two to one lost support about twice as fast as those where supporters held that edge. Co-author Thad Kousser explained: "if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp."
- **Low early support and failure:** The article doesn't directly test whether measures polling low early were likelier to fail. Its closest finding is that measures with more undecided responses before the vote showed no clear difference in losing support or failing. The article says the "cautious voter" theory is hard to confirm without asking individual voters. Across the full set, 35% passed.
- **Why declines happen:** PPIC survey director Dean Bonner pointed to timing: "Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it's starting off without there being a 'No' campaign."

**Prop 40 money snapshot (reporting from mid-October through Nov. 2):**

- **Measure:** Residents with more than $1 billion in net worth would face a one-time 5% levy, and public health would receive roughly nine-tenths of the proceeds.
- **Yes side:** Forbes puts the union's fundraising at about $32 million, less than a tenth of what the opposition has amassed. That union is SEIU-UHW.
- **No-side totals:** A Capital & Main review pegs Building a Better California's spending at more than $304 million. That committee supplies about 96% of opposition money. Forbes, citing The Guardian, says the overall fight has taken in over $340 million.
- **Brin and other donors:** Brin is the opposition's largest single backer, at about $102 million. Washington Post reporting tallies his giving at over $100 million. Forbes lists John Doerr among the top donors against the tax, at about $40 million.
- **Ads and polls:** The Post's review finds the wealthy opposition has out-advertised the measure's backers by more than 250 to 1. Recent surveys register slipping support as spending climbs. Union head Dave Regan projects opponents will spend at least $400 million by Election Day.

The $304 million figure is money spent, while the $340 million figure is money raised, and they come from different outlets, so they aren't directly comparable. These are press tallies, so check state campaign finance filings before relying on exact totals.

No ppic.org page appeared in these results, so the points below come from news coverage of the late-October PPIC survey.

- Yes sits at 46% and No at 52%, with 2% undecided, based on 1,086 likely voters. Interviews were held online in English and Spanish. No holds a six-point edge.
- Yahoo News dates the release to Oct. 28, while CalMatters says the survey was published on a Tuesday (Oct. 27).
- Support has slipped since September, when the measure narrowly led 52% to 46%.
- One Yahoo News piece, however, lists the earlier PPIC result as 43% yes and 55% no, which conflicts with other coverage.
- Yes support runs above 60% among Democrats, around 40% among independents, and roughly 20% among Republicans.
- Backing runs especially high among voters aged 18 to 34 (70%), people earning under $40,000 (64%), Latino voters (58%), and Los Angeles residents (53%).
- Props 41 and 42, which would nullify Prop 40, have moved ahead of it in polling. CalMatters, by contrast, describes the pair as a near toss-up.
- Passage requires a vote above 50%, and Prop 40 would be triggered only if voters reject Props 41 and 42, which clash with it.
- Politico's early-October poll had Yes ahead, 46% to 43%, which runs against PPIC's reading.

The results don't report a margin of error for the October PPIC poll, so verify the details against ppic.org directly.
